patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia with unusual anticoagulation history
patient.hpi:
A 44-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted to the neurology ward for evaluation of fluctuating diplopia, bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, dysphonia, and fatigable chewing. Symptoms were characteristically worse at the end of meals and at the end of the day, and improved significantly with rest. She had noticed progressive worsening over 8 weeks, with diplopia initially present only on right lateral gaze, subsequently becoming present throughout the day. She described difficulty chewing through a full meal without tiring, nasal voice quality when reading aloud for more than a few minutes, and increasing difficulty swallowing pills over the past 2 weeks.

Her past medical history was notable for antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), diagnosed 6 years ago following three consecutive spontaneous first-trimester abortions. She also had a history of transient hypothyroidism following a viral illness 4 years ago that resolved without treatment. She was taking aspirin 81 mg daily for APS-related thromboprophylaxis. She had no prior neurological diagnosis.

On examination, she demonstrated progressive fatigability of upward gaze during a prolonged Simpson test. Ptosis was bilaterally present (left greater than right) and worsened with sustained upgaze. She had dysarthria and weakness of facial and neck muscles. Tongue strength was mildly reduced but symmetric. The Cogan lid twitch sign was positive. Ice pack test produced a 3 mm improvement bilaterally in 5 minutes. Limb strength was 5/5 throughout with normal coordination and sensation.

The antiphospholipid syndrome history raised initial concern for cerebrovascular disease as a possible explanatory framework — specifically, a small basilar artery TIA producing bilateral ocular motor signs. Laboratory results were notable for elevated anticardiolipin antibodies and anti-β2-glycoprotein-I antibodies consistent with her known APS, and prolonged PTT attributed to lupus anticoagulant.
pmh: Antiphospholipid syndrome — three spontaneous abortions; anticardiolipin and anti-β2-GP1 antibodies positive
Transient hypothyroidism 4 years ago (viral thyroiditis), resolved without treatment
No known autoimmune or rheumatological co-diagnosis

family_history: Mother had rheumatoid arthritis. No family history of neuromuscular disease.

social_history.note: Accountant; married; two children by IVF after APS diagnosis; non-smoker; minimal alcohol; physically active prior to symptom onset

physical_exam.general: Alert, well-nourished woman; mild bilateral ptosis visible; no distress
physical_exam.neurological: Bilateral ptosis (left > right); worsens with sustained upgaze (positive Simpson test). Cogan lid twitch positive. Ice pack test: 3 mm improvement bilaterally. Diplopia on right lateral gaze. Extraocular movements: mild abduction limitation right eye. Dysarthria (nasal component). Facial muscle weakness (bilateral, mild). Neck flexor strength 4+/5 (fatigable). Limb strength 5/5 throughout. Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. No fasciculations. Normal coordination.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft; mild tenderness right iliac fossa (not acutely relevant); no organomegaly

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Seronegative generalized myasthenia gravis in a patient with antiphospholipid syndrome (G70.01)

differential.key_features: Normal brain MRI/MRA; no DWI restriction; fatigable symptoms with diurnal variation (not typical TIA); TIA is fixed deficit not fatigable pattern
differential.distinguishing_test: Brain MRI with DWI (normal) and MRA (normal) exclude vascular etiology

differential.key_features: Normal brain MRI; no periventricular or juxtacortical lesions; no McDonald criteria met; fatigable symptoms rather than relapses
differential.distinguishing_test: Brain MRI (no demyelinating lesions); CSF (not needed given MRI normal)

differential.key_features: Anti-ds-DNA negative; normal complement; does not meet SLE criteria; positive ANA is low-titer non-specific
Ocular and bulbar predominance (not typical LEMS); no 50Hz increment on RNS; no proximal limb weakness or absent reflexes

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with MRA to exclude cerebrovascular event (TIA) given APS history
RNS at low rate (3 Hz) in multiple muscle groups to identify NMJ dysfunction
MG antibody panel — AChR and anti-MuSK (may be negative in seronegative MG)
SFEMG — most sensitive test for seronegative MG; provides electrophysiological confirmation
Initiate pyridostigmine; add prednisone with PPI; plan azathioprine (after TPMT testing); discuss MGTX trial thymectomy evidence

critical_actions: Do not attribute fatigable bilateral ocular motor signs solely to APS-related TIA without normal brain MRI/MRA
Recognize seronegative MG — negative AChR and anti-MuSK does not exclude diagnosis; SFEMG is required
SFEMG is the confirmatory test of choice in seronegative MG
Note lupus anticoagulant as cause of elevated aPTT (laboratory artifact, not true coagulopathy requiring treatment change)
Screen for thymoma despite seronegative status
contraindicated_actions: Do not assume negative MG antibodies exclude MG — seronegative MG exists and requires SFEMG
Do not escalate anticoagulation based on elevated aPTT alone in known APS (it is a lab artifact from lupus anticoagulant)
Do not use fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides in any future infection management
Do not increase aspirin to full anticoagulation without confirmed APS thrombotic event
key_reasoning_points: The diagnostic puzzle: APS history diverts attention to cerebrovascular TIA as the explanation for bilateral ocular motor signs
Fatigable ptosis with diurnal variation and positive ice pack test distinguishes MG from TIA (TIA causes sudden, fixed deficits)
Seronegative MG (negative AChR and MuSK) occurs in ~15% of generalized MG; SFEMG is >97% sensitive
Elevated aPTT from lupus anticoagulant is a laboratory artifact — does not represent true clotting abnormality requiring treatment escalation
Polyautoimmune background (APS, subclinical Hashimoto's) increases overall autoimmune disease risk including MG
RNS abnormality in multiple muscle groups (cranial and distal) confirms GENERALIZED MG, not ocular-only

red_herrings.finding: Antiphospholipid syndrome with positive lupus anticoagulant — TIA concern
red_herrings.why_misleading: APS is a known cause of stroke and TIA; bilateral ocular motor signs + APS history creates strong anchoring to vascular diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal brain MRI/MRA excludes TIA; fatigable, diurnal symptoms are incompatible with vascular etiology

red_herrings.why_misleading: Elevated aPTT typically triggers investigation for bleeding diathesis or factor deficiency
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Elevated aPTT is from lupus anticoagulant (in vitro artifact); mixing study shows inhibitor pattern; no true coagulopathy

red_herrings.why_misleading: Negative AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 antibodies might lead clinician to abandon MG diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seronegative MG (~15% of generalized cases); SFEMG is the required next step with >97% sensitivity

metadata.condition_name: Seronegative generalized myasthenia gravis with antiphospholipid syndrome
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: APS history misdirects to TIA as explanation; seronegative MG requires SFEMG for confirmation; elevated aPTT from lupus anticoagulant is a laboratory red herring

mri.impression: Normal MRI/MRA; no infarction, no vasculopathy; APS-related cerebrovascular disease excluded. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings:
ELECTROCARDIOGRAM

Patient: 44-year-old female
Indication: Pre-investigation baseline; valvular lesions may occur in APS

RHYTHM: Sinus rhythm at 78 bpm
INTERVALS: PR 158 ms, QRS 82 ms, QTc 408 ms

INTERPRETATION: Normal sinus rhythm; no arrhythmia; normal QTc. No ischemic ST-T changes.

CONCLUSION: Normal ECG.

additional_observations:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: New MG diagnosis — exclude thymoma

TECHNIQUE: CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm slices

FINDINGS:
  ANTERIOR MEDIASTINUM: No thymic mass. Thymic region shows age-appropriate fatty replacement.
  LUNGS: Clear. No parenchymal disease.
  MEDIASTINUM: No adenopathy.
  HEART/PERICARDIUM: Normal.

IMPRESSION:
1. No thymoma or anterior mediastinal mass.
2. Normal chest CT.

NOTE: In APS, cardiac valvular lesions (Libman-Sacks endocarditis) may occur; no valvular abnormality was visible on CT. Echocardiography is recommended for more sensitive valvular evaluation.
ct.impression: No thymoma; normal chest CT; echocardiography recommended for APS valvular assessment

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Bilateral ocular motor findings, fatigable weakness; exclude NMJ disorder

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS at orbicularis oculi, abductor digiti minimi, deltoid

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi (facial nerve): Decrement 17% (1st to 4th stimulus) [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Abductor digiti minimi (ulnar nerve): Decrement 13% ABNORMAL
  Deltoid: Decrement 10% BORDERLINE ABNORMAL

NOTE: Abnormal decremental response in both cranial and distal muscles confirms generalized NMJ dysfunction.

CONCLUSION: Electrophysiological NMJ dysfunction consistent with generalized myasthenia gravis.

output.impression: RNS: 17% decrement orbicularis, 13% abductor digiti minimi, 10% deltoid — generalized NMJ dysfunction, confirms MG

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — ORBICULARIS OCULI

Indication: Seronegative MG confirmation

RESULTS:
  MCD: 66 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 26% of potential pairs
  Fiber density: 1.8 (normal ≤2.0)

CONCLUSION: Markedly increased jitter and blocking confirms NMJ dysfunction. In seronegative MG, SFEMG provides the electrophysiological confirmation needed for diagnosis. Sensitivity >97% for generalized MG.

output.impression: SFEMG: MCD 66 µs with 26% blocking — definitively confirms NMJ dysfunction; seronegative MG established

findings:
ECHOCARDIOGRAM — TRANSTHORACIC

Indication: APS with positive lupus anticoagulant; screen for Libman-Sacks endocarditis

FINDINGS:
  LEFT VENTRICLE: Normal size and systolic function; EF 62%
  VALVES: No thickening of mitral or aortic valves. No vegetations. No mitral regurgitation. Mild tricuspid regurgitation (trivial) — normal variant.
  CHAMBERS: Normal right and left atrial size.
  PERICARDIUM: No effusion.
  DOPPLER: Normal pulmonary artery pressure.

IMPRESSION:
1. Normal echocardiogram. No Libman-Sacks lesions.
2. Normal cardiac function.
3. No cardioembolic source for cerebrovascular events.

NOTE: APS cardiac complications include valve lesions and thrombotic events; neither is identified here. MG diagnosis is unrelated to cardiac structure.
output.impression: Normal echocardiogram; no Libman-Sacks endocarditis; no cardioembolic source

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Antiphospholipid Syndrome and Myasthenia Gravis Co-occurrence

KEY FINDINGS:
1. APS-MG ASSOCIATION: Co-occurrence of APS and MG is documented in the literature; both are autoimmune conditions and can co-exist in polyautoimmune individuals. APS does not cause MG; they occur concurrently.
2. SERONEGATIVE MG IN POLYAUTOIMMUNE CONTEXT: Patients with APS/SLE may have higher rates of seronegative MG; anti-LRP4 antibodies and clustered glycine receptor antibodies may be detected on extended panels not routinely available.
3. LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT AND COAGULATION: Lupus anticoagulant prolongs aPTT in vitro (laboratory artifact); does not cause bleeding. Do not increase anticoagulation based on elevated aPTT alone in APS.
4. THYMECTOMY IN SERONEGATIVE MG: MGTX trial benefits may be less clear in seronegative patients; however, thymectomy is still recommended by some guidelines. CT chest showed no thymoma here.
5. IMMUNOSUPPRESSION STRATEGY: Prednisone and azathioprine are first-line. Mycophenolate mofetil is an alternative. Important: check if APS requires anticoagulation escalation before immunosuppression.

CONCLUSION: APS and seronegative MG can co-exist; diagnosis of MG confirmed by electrophysiology; immunosuppression appropriate.
output.summary: APS and MG can co-exist in polyautoimmune patients; elevated aPTT from lupus anticoagulant is lab artifact; SFEMG confirms seronegative MG

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — PREDNISONE AND AZATHIOPRINE IN APS + MG

Query: Immunosuppression for MG in patient with APS on aspirin

FINDINGS:
  PREDNISONE + ASPIRIN:
  - Additive GI mucosal irritation risk — consider PPI (omeprazole 20 mg daily) prophylaxis
  - Prednisone may transiently worsen MG at initiation (well-documented); start at 10-20 mg/day and titrate slowly

  AZATHIOPRINE + APS:
  - No direct pharmacokinetic interaction with aspirin
  - Azathioprine may have mild antiplatelet properties — monitor platelet count
  - Myelosuppression monitoring required (CBC monthly for 3 months, then quarterly)
  - TPMT genotyping recommended before azathioprine initiation

  WARFARIN (if needed for APS thrombosis):
  - If warfarin required in future: azathioprine may modestly reduce warfarin effect
  - Monitor INR more frequently when adding azathioprine

CONCLUSION: Prednisone + azathioprine safe in this patient; add PPI; check TPMT before azathioprine; monitor CBC.
output.summary: PPI needed with prednisone + aspirin; TPMT genotyping before azathioprine; monitor CBC; no major APS-MG drug interaction
